fields.title: Kedr: Three Deals Stuck on One Objection
fields.summary: The sales team is sure a feature is missing. Customers say otherwise. Decide what to do.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you do this quarter and why?
fields.brief/company: Kedr is a cloud warehouse management service for small distributors. 140 customers, average bill of 40 thousand per month, sales cycle of about two months.
fields.brief/context: Three deals that are large for us have been stuck for two months. The head of sales believes the lack of 1C integration is blocking them and asks to schedule it for this quarter. The integration requires six weeks of development. Quarter planning is in one week.
fields.brief/objective: Understand what is actually blocking the deals and decide how to spend the quarter.
fields.brief/constraints: Three developers. Sales team of four, closing about six deals a month.
fields.brief/task: Decide what you will do this quarter and justify your choice.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: An objection is a risk, not a feature debate
fields.learnTakeaway/body: When a deal is stuck, the temptation is to hear a feature request and start building. But the person signing the contract isn't risking features: they risk warehouse downtime, unrecovered costs, or having to justify the decision to their boss. Three identical 'we'll think about it' responses usually hide three different risks. They are resolved with three different answers, none of which require six weeks of development.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
All three are distributors with 20–40 warehouse employees.

Deal A. We spoke with the warehouse manager, who is thrilled. The owner signs the contract, but we haven't spoken to them once. The reason for the pause: 'we need to consult.'

Deal B. The owner asked directly: 'what if the warehouse stops during the transition?' The salesperson replied that implementation takes two weeks and everything will be set up for them.

Deal C. The owner said it's 'expensive.' In previous emails, the same owner wrote that they lose about 90 thousand a month on inventory errors.

Only one of the three deals (Deal A) asked about 1C, and that was in the context of: 'is there an export to accounting?'
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Standard scenario: thirty minutes going through sections—receiving, placement, shipping, reports, permissions, integrations.

Data on the demo environment: 'Product 1', 'Product 2', a warehouse with 50 items.

Out of 18 demos this quarter, 5 deals closed. All five successful deals shared a common trait noticed by one salesperson: before the meeting, he asked what their pain points were and showed a single scenario instead of an overview.

Error scenarios—like inventory discrepancies or shipping cancellations—are not shown in demos: 'we don't want to show things breaking.'
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
The head of sales in a presentation: 'the warehouse software market is 20 billion, we need 1%.'

Your bottom-up calculation: there are about 9,000 distributors with 5–50 warehouse employees in the country. About half are already automated and won't change systems in the coming years. That leaves about 4,500 × 40 thousand × 12 = 2.2 billion per year.

A sales team of four closes 6 deals a month. In two years, that's 144 customers, or about 69 million per year.

So with the current channel, you will capture 3% of the addressable segment in two years. The market is not the constraint.
fields.evidenceCards/3/title: What is Requested vs What is Possible
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
1C integration—six weeks, affects billing and permissions.

Parallel operation with the old system for the first month (data written to both)—one and a half weeks.

One-click upload of customer inventory list to the demo environment—three days.

Inventory discrepancy handling scenario in the demo—already in the product, but not yet shown.

Head of sales: 'If we have 1C, we'll close all three.' When asked which of the three asked for it, he replied, 'everyone asks sooner or later.'
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Mitigate transition risk and redesign the demo
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Address the three objections as risks of specific people, build parallel operation with the old system, learn to show a single scenario using customer data, and include an edge case in the demo.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
Parallel operation is released in one and a half weeks. Deal B closes in three weeks: the owner was worried about warehouse downtime, not the implementation timeline, and now has an answer.
In Deal C, you present a calculation: 90 thousand in losses from inventory errors vs 40 thousand for the subscription. The deal closes—'expensive' meant 'I don't understand what I'll get.'
In Deal A, you reach out to the owner directly and prepare materials for the warehouse manager to present. The deal moves forward but only closes next quarter.
Uploading inventory to the demo environment takes three days; 9 out of the next 20 demos close, compared to the previous 5.
1C integration is scheduled for next quarter, based on actual demand.
Trade-off: you didn't build what sales requested loudest and spent two weeks on conversations and minor fixes.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: The sales team works with customers daily and asks for the same thing. Dedicate six weeks and resolve the issue.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
The integration is released in seven weeks. Deal A closes—the export to accounting was actually needed there.
Deals B and C don't budge: one is worried about warehouse downtime, the other about ROI, and neither has anything to do with 1C. Both are lost by the end of the quarter.
16 deals close during the quarter instead of the usual 18: demos didn't change, and development was busy.
A quarter later, the head of sales asks for another feature using the same 'everyone asks' justification.
Trade-off: you closed one out of three deals at the cost of a quarter and left the issues repeated in all eighteen demos untouched.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Offer a discount and close the quarter
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: The 'expensive' objection was stated directly. Offer a 20% discount for the first year to all three deals and close them now.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
Deal C closes with a discount. Deals A and B do not: their objections were not about price.
Six months later, customer C asks why their rate went up and enters renewal negotiations demanding a discount.
Word of the discount spreads to other customers: two existing ones ask for the same rate.
Upon review, you find that 'expensive' for owner C meant 'I don't understand what I'll get'—even though the ROI calculation was in their own emails.
Trade-off: you bought one deal at the expense of margin and future pricing without finding out what the objection was actually about.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Move upmarket to a larger segment
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Three deals with 20–40 employees have been dragging for two months. Direct sales to larger companies with higher average bills.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The pivot takes a quarter. The average bill in the new segment is three times higher, but the sales cycle is six months or longer, and it requires implementation experience the team lacks.
One deal closes during the quarter instead of eighteen. Revenue drops.
Upon review, the bottom-up calculation is recalled: there are 4,500 addressable customers in the current segment, and you have captured 140. The constraint was not market size, but the fact that four salespeople physically close six deals a month.
Trade-off: you tried to solve a growth ceiling by switching segments when no ceiling existed yet.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: An objection was mistaken for a feature debate rather than an expressed risk
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Failing to distinguish between users and decision-makers
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: The demo focuses on product sections rather than the customer's problem
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Showing only the happy path, without any edge cases
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: Segment size was calculated top-down as a percentage of a large report
fields.rubric/remediation/5/gap: Looking for a growth ceiling in the market without checking the sales methodology
